stances.claim: CJP is glad the SC is speeding up the legal proceedings on the Binay-Morales suspension -- the new unprecedented procedure (Baguio oral argument, 30-page position papers with table of authorities, interpellation-first format) is a laudable reform aimed at resolving the rather embarrassing chaos of two bickering mayors in the nation's financial capital
To be fair and objective in this sub-judice case that will probably split the Court, CJP will just summarize the relevant facts, main issues, and arguments -- not opine on outcome

The factual chronology shows an extraordinary speed: March 5 complaint, March 10 suspension order issued without waiting for counteraffidavit, March 16 implementation by wall-posting at 8:30 AM (all gates closed), 9:47 AM Vice Mayor Peña oath as acting mayor, ~noon CA 60-day TRO grant, then a March 25 Morales SC petition to annul the CA TRO and stop CA contempt proceedings

Morales argues: Constitution Art XI Sec 13 mandates her investigative function; Sec 14 of the Ombudsman Law prohibits courts from issuing writs of injunction to delay her investigation; suspension is not a penalty but an 'aid to investigation' to prevent Binay from using his office to influence witnesses and tamper with evidence (practically all documentary evidence is in city-government custody and witnesses are in city employ)

Morales further argues she is removable only by impeachment, cannot be held in contempt because contempt penalties (fine, imprisonment) are criminal in nature, and impeachable officers are criminally liable only after serving their terms

Binay counters: Morales' power is not absolute; it is subject to the constitutional duty of courts to strike down grave abuse of discretion -- and Morales gravely abused her discretion because the complaint itself showed the irregular acts were allegedly done prior to his incumbent term, invoking the condonation doctrine: 'a public official cannot be removed for administrative misconduct committed during a prior term; his reelection to office operates as a condonation of the officer's previous misconduct'; payments during his present term were mere implementations of the prior-term contract

On the contempt issue, Binay invokes Philippine Guardians v. Comelec (March 22, 2011), which ruled that the Comelec -- composed of impeachable officials -- was guilty of contempt for failing to comply with a status-quo order, defeating Morales' impeachable-officer immunity argument

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes that he is glad the Supreme Court is speeding up the legal proceedings involving the suspension of Makati Mayor Jejomar Erwin S. Binay Jr. by Ombudsman Conchita Carpio Morales. Aside from immediately setting oral argument at 2 PM Tuesday in Baguio City, the Court abbreviated the process by requiring the parties to file at noon tomorrow a position paper not exceeding 30 pages backed by a 'table of authorities'; the hearing will begin not with the usual oral presentations but with the justices' interpellation, first of Morales' counsel and then of Binay's. This unprecedented procedure is clearly a reform measure aimed at speeding up proceedings -- justices study position papers in advance and just ask questions to clarify, test, and validate them -- and signals their laudable determination to resolve speedily the rather embarrassing chaos of having two bickering mayors in the nation's financial capital. To be fair and objective in this sub-judice case that will probably split the Court, CJ summarizes the relevant facts, main issues, and arguments. On March 5, 2015, a special panel of investigators submitted a complaint alleging Binay and several others violated the Anti-Graft Law in the construction of the Makati City Hall Parking Building. Morales directed Binay to file his counteraffidavit. On March 10, 2015, without waiting for the counteraffidavit, Morales issued a suspension order placing Binay and 20 others under preventive suspension for not more than six months. This order was implemented by the DILG at 8:30 AM on March 16 by posting it on the wall of the Makati City Hall ('given that all the gates of the Makati City Hall were closed'); at 9:47 AM the same day, Vice Mayor Romulo V. Peña took his oath as acting mayor. Acting on Binay's certiorari petition filed March 11, the Court of Appeals issued a resolution at 'around noon' on March 16 granting a 60-day temporary restraining order. Morales filed a 'manifestation' in the CA arguing that given prior service and implementation of the suspension order 'there is no more act to be restrained by the TRO as it has become moot and academic' and that the TRO was textually vague. Binay then petitioned the CA to hold Morales in contempt for refusing to obey the TRO; the CA directed Morales to comment within three days. On March 25, Morales asked the SC to annul the CA's TRO and stop the CA from adjudicating Binay's contempt petition. Morales argues that the Constitution (Art XI, Sec 13) mandates her 'to investigate any act or omission [that] appears to be illegal, unjust, improper or inefficient,' and that Sec 14 of the Ombudsman Law states 'No writ of injunction shall be issued by any court to delay an investigation being conducted by the Ombudsman.' Binay's suspension is an essential part of her investigation; the CA's TRO illegally delays it. Citing settled jurisprudence, she argues suspension is not a penalty but an 'aid to investigation' to prevent Binay from using the powers and prerogatives of his office to influence potential witnesses -- practically all the documentary evidence is in the city government's custody and potential witnesses are in the city's employ, so there is an imperative need to guard against tampering and intimidation. Morales also contends that as a public officer removable only by impeachment, she cannot be held in contempt because the penalties for contempt are fine and imprisonment, which are criminal in nature, and impeachable officers are criminally liable only after serving their terms. In his comment, Binay avers that Morales' power to investigate and suspend is not absolute; it is subject to the constitutional duty of courts to strike down grave abuse of discretion. Morales gravely abused her discretion because, by merely looking at the complaint, she would have known the irregular acts allegedly against him were done prior to his incumbent term -- invoking the condonation doctrine: 'a public official cannot be removed for administrative misconduct committed during a prior term; his reelection to office operates as a condonation of the officer's previous misconduct to the extent of cutting off the right to remove him therefor.' Payments made during his present term were mere implementations of the building contract entered during his prior term, condoned by the electorate. On the contempt issue, Binay maintains that impeachable officials may be held liable, per Philippine Guardians v. Comelec (March 22, 2011), which ruled that the Comelec -- composed of impeachable officials -- was guilty of contempt for failing to comply with a status-quo order.
